units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally explain one reason why a cat is living and a rock is not.
units.task: Introduce the concepts of living and non-living things. Discuss observable traits like needing food, growing, and moving on their own. Create a class chart sorting pictures of a cat, a rock, a tree, and a car.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can state that a color change like rust indicates a chemical property.
units.task: Show a shiny iron nail and a rusty iron nail. Explain that the color change is evidence of a chemical property reacting to the environment (air/water). Discuss how this is different from just painting the nail.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally identify which side of the balance scale holds the object with more mass.
units.task: Introduce the balance scale. Demonstrate how placing objects in the cups causes the scale to tip. Show that the side that goes down has more mass. Compare an apple and a grape as a class.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can correctly align the zero mark of a ruler with the edge of an object during guided practice.
units.task: Demonstrate how to use a ruler to measure length in centimeters. Show how to align the zero mark with the edge of the object. Measure a pencil and a book as a class, writing the results with the cm unit.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally state at least two descriptive words for a given object.
units.task: Introduce the concept of qualitative properties by showing a wooden block, a plastic cup, and a metal spoon. Guide students to describe how each looks, feels, and smells. Write their descriptive words on the board and explain that these are called properties.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can match the term malleability to flat objects and ductility to wires.
units.task: Introduce malleability by flattening a piece of clay or foil, and ductility by showing a copper wire. Explain the definitions and have students repeat the terms while doing hand motions (pressing flat, pulling long).

units.mastery_criterion: Students can define conductor as allowing electricity to pass and insulator as blocking it.
units.task: Build a simple circuit using a 1.5V AA battery, two wires, and a small LED bulb. Leave a gap in the wires. Test a metal paperclip to close the gap (light turns on) and a plastic spoon (light stays off). Introduce the terms conductor and insulator.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can identify which object makes a dark shadow and which lets light through.
units.task: Use a strong flashlight in a darkened room. Shine it through a clear glass cup, a piece of wax paper, and a thick book. Ask students to observe what happens to the light and the shadow on the wall behind each object. Introduce transparent, translucent, and opaque.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally identify which objects require batteries or a plug to function.
units.task: Introduce electrical and non-electrical devices by showing a battery-operated toy car and a wooden push car. Discuss what makes each move. Show pictures of household items and sort them on the board into 'needs electricity' and 'does not need electricity'.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally describe that the battery makes the fan blades move.
units.task: Show a battery-operated fan turning on (electrical to mechanical) and a wind-up toy moving (potential to kinetic). Discuss how energy doesn't disappear but changes its job. Create a simple anchor chart with arrows showing the changes.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can state that white light is made of many colors.
units.task: In a dark room, shine a flashlight through a glass prism onto a white wall to create a rainbow. Discuss how the white light from the flashlight is actually made of many colors, and the prism breaks them apart.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can state that mixing base colors creates new colors.
units.task: Demonstrate mixing primary paint colors (cyan, magenta, yellow) in clear cups of water. Show how mixing two colors creates a new color (e.g., yellow and cyan make green). Explain that this is how printers make all the colors in a picture.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can explain that the sun's heat caused the ice to melt into liquid water.
units.task: Place an ice cube in a sealed plastic bag in a sunny window and another in a dark, cool closet. Ask students to predict what will happen. Check back later to see the melted ice. Discuss how adding heat changes solid to liquid, and conceptually discuss boiling water to make gas.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can identify red as danger/stop and green as safe/go.
units.task: Show large images of local traffic signs (red stop sign) and school emergency exit signs (green). Discuss what the colors mean (red = stop/danger, green = safe/go). Ask students why it is important that everyone agrees on what these colors mean.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can state that the ball dropped from higher up made a bigger hole because it had more energy.
units.task: Discuss amusement park rides like a slide (tobogán). Ask why sliding from a higher point makes you go faster. Demonstrate dropping a heavy plastic ball into a deep tray of flour from 10 cm and then from 50 cm. Discuss how the higher drop gave the ball more energy, creating a larger crater, just like starting higher on a slide gives more energy.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can define revolution as Earth's path around the Sun and state it takes one year or 365 days.
units.task: Explain Earth's revolution around the Sun. Place a large yellow ball (Sun) in the center of the room. Walk a smaller globe around the Sun in a large circle, explaining this path is the orbit and takes 365 days (1 year).

units.mastery_criterion: Students can point to the skewer and identify it as the model's axis, and describe that Earth spins on a similar imaginary line.
units.task: Use a teacher-preassembled globe or foam-ball model with a blunt paper-tube axis. Demonstrate rotation and point to the imaginary axis. Students do not pierce or assemble the model.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can name at least one human threat and one corresponding protective action.
units.task: Discuss human threats to wildlife (e.g., littering, feeding) and introduce concrete conservation actions.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can define the three diet types based on the pictures shown.
units.task: Introduce herbivores, carnivores, and omnivores using pictures of animals and their typical meals.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can explain that domestic animals rely on humans while wild animals survive in nature.
units.task: Define domestic vs. wild animals, focusing on human care and natural habitats, using picture examples.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can point to the correct body part on a model when a locomotion type is named.
units.task: Introduce locomotion types (swim, fly, walk) and corresponding body parts (fins, wings, legs) using animal models.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can state that mushrooms absorb food while plants make it.
units.task: Compare a mushroom and a plant using photos, focusing on how they get food (making it vs absorbing it).

units.mastery_criterion: Students can name one useful and one harmful aspect of fungi.
units.task: Introduce the uses of fungi (e.g., food, medicine) and their potential harms (e.g., diseases, toxicity) using pictures.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can identify the category for each of the three examples provided.
units.task: Introduce categories of plant utility (food, medicine, raw materials) using real examples like cotton, mint, and corn.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can point to and name the roots, stem, and leaves on the live plant.
units.task: Introduce the basic parts of a plant (roots, stem, leaves) using a live potted plant.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can identify food and oxygen as the outputs of the process shown on the board.
units.task: Explain photosynthesis outputs using a felt board model showing sunlight entering and food/oxygen being produced.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully assemble the device and demonstrate that twisting the rubber band causes it to roll.
units.task: Guide students to build a rolling device using CDs, a cardboard tube, and rubber bands. Demonstrate how twisting the rubber band stores energy for motion.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully cut straws to the correct length and pack them so they do not fall out when the can is inverted.
units.task: Demonstrate how to measure and cut paper straws to the length of a recycled can, and pack them tightly inside to create hollow spaces for insects.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally state the difference between domestic and wild animals based on human reliance.
units.task: Present images of common animals. Explain the difference between domestic (rely on humans) and wild (survive independently). Sort a few examples together on the board.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully assemble a hanger balance that hangs level when empty.
units.task: Guide students step-by-step to build a balance using a clothes hanger, string, and two cups. Demonstrate how to find equilibrium using identical marbles.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully replicate the layers (rocks, then soil) and plant their specimen securely.
units.task: Demonstrate how to layer small rocks for drainage, add soil, and carefully plant a small specimen in a clear plastic container to create a terrarium.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can articulate that the folded bridge holds more weight and identify the folds as the reason for increased strength.
units.task: Demonstrate how to build a flat paper bridge and a fan-folded paper bridge between two books. Show how to add coins to the center until collapse.

units.mastery_criterion: Students explicitly link the visual observation of the melting wax to the generation of heat, stating that electrical energy from the battery transforms into thermal energy.
units.task: Perform a teacher-led demonstration connecting a battery to a pencil lead with a small piece of wax on it. Have students observe the wax melting as a visual indicator of heat and identify the energy change.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully wrap the string, mark it accurately, and read the measurement on the ruler within 1 cm of accuracy.
units.task: Demonstrate how to wrap a string around a spherical fruit, mark the meeting point, and measure the string segment with a ruler. Have students replicate the process with an orange.

units.mastery_criterion: Student states that the roots hold the soil, preventing it from washing away.
units.task: Relate the activity to local issues like landslides in Nejapa or sedimentation of the the supplied location River. Set up three plastic bottle halves: one with bare soil, one with dead leaves, one with live plants. Pour equal amounts of water through each. Ask students to observe the runoff water color and infer why the plant bottle has clear water, protecting the 'hillside'.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can correctly identify the bin for an apple core and a plastic bottle during the demonstration.
units.task: Introduce the concepts of biodegradable (nature breaks it down) and non-biodegradable (nature cannot easily break it down). Show clean examples of each and sort them into two labeled bins as a class.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can state that vaccines help make defenses to fight sickness.
units.task: Explain vaccines using a metaphor: the body is a castle, and vaccines are training for the guards (defenses) so they know how to fight off invaders (sickness).

units.mastery_criterion: Student can verbally state that the tower is the hazard and standing close is the risk.
units.task: Use a teacher-prepared diagram of a tall unstable block tower and objects placed near or far from it. Distinguish the possible falling event from the exposure of an object to that event. Do not shake or climb a real structure.

units.mastery_criterion: Student successfully demonstrates dropping, covering their head/neck, and holding onto a sturdy object.
units.task: Demonstrate the 'Drop, Cover, and Hold on' technique for earthquakes. Explain each step clearly. Have students practice the motion step-by-step under their desks.

units.mastery_criterion: Student points to and names at least three objects that pose a risk in the poster.
units.task: Display a large poster of a messy classroom. Guide students to point out objects that could cause someone to trip, fall, or get hurt. Discuss why each identified object is a risk.

units.mastery_criterion: Student identifies that not washing hands after the bathroom was the poor hygiene practice.
units.task: Read a short story about a character who forgets to wash their hands after using the bathroom and gets a stomach ache. Discuss the specific action that caused the illness.

units.mastery_criterion: Student reasons that hands must be washed with soap to remove invisible organisms that spread.
units.task: Rub a drop of cooking oil and a pinch of ground cinnamon on a student's hand to represent invisible organisms. Have them try to wash it off with just water, then with soap and water. Discuss why soap is needed to break down the oils that trap dirt and germs, justifying the need for proper handwashing.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can point to the foods that require cooking when asked.
units.task: Show pictures of raw chicken, raw beans, and an apple. Explain that while the apple can be washed and eaten raw, the chicken and beans must be cooked to be safe to eat.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can repeat the four essential qualities (grow, reproduce, move, feed) when prompted.
units.task: Explicitly teach the essential qualities of living things: they grow, reproduce, move, and feed. Use a simple story of a puppy growing into a dog, eating food, moving around, and having puppies to illustrate these points.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can explain that quantitative properties use numbers and qualitative properties use descriptive words.
units.task: Explain the difference between qualitative (words/senses) and quantitative (numbers/measurements) properties. Create a T-chart on the board and sort examples like red, 10 cm, heavy, and 5 grams as a class.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can state that the extra 6 hours each year add up to a full 24-hour day every four years.
units.task: Explain that Earth's orbit actually takes 365 days and about 6 hours. Use 4 blocks, each representing 6 hours. Show that over 4 years, these blocks add up to 24 hours, creating one extra day (leap year).

units.mastery_criterion: Students can name the dry and rainy seasons and identify one visual difference (e.g., green vs brown vegetation).
units.task: Compare a twelve-month rainfall chart with two landscape image sequences. Identify sustained drier and wetter periods using repeated observations rather than a single day.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can verbally identify which side of the globe is experiencing day and which is experiencing night during the demonstration.
units.task: Darken the room and use a flashlight to represent the Sun and a globe for Earth. Shine the light on one side of the globe, explaining that the lit side is day and the dark side is night. Slowly rotate the globe to show the cycle.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can point to the roots and stem on a diagram and state their functions in water transport.
units.task: Introduce plant roots and stems using a pre-prepared celery stalk in colored water to demonstrate water transport.

units.mastery_criterion: Students verbally identify the quiet garden and reason that insects avoid human disturbance.
units.task: Discuss why insects need quiet places. Show pictures of a busy playground and a quiet garden corner, asking students to infer which is better for an insect hotel and why.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can describe the first thing that comes out of a seed (the root).
units.task: Explain the process of seed germination. Show a time-lapse video (if possible) or a series of large posters showing a seed sprouting roots, then a stem, then leaves. Set up a class demonstration of a bean in a clear cup with wet paper towels.

units.mastery_criterion: One point for the correct stimulus-response match and one for identifying the before/after evidence; both are required.
units.task: Use only teacher-supplied picture pairs and fictional before/after records. Match a supplied change in lighting or movement with the response shown in two fictional records. Cite one visible change.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can explain that too much water makes the soil loose, leading to landslides during the rainy season.
units.task: Discuss how intense rain during the rainy season can cause natural hazards like floods and landslides. Show a simple physical model: pour water over a mound of loose soil in a tray to demonstrate a landslide.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can state that the Sun appears in the East in the morning because of the direction Earth spins.
units.task: Explain that Earth rotates from West to East. Use a globe and a stationary light source to show how a specific point on the globe enters the light from the East first, making the Sun appear to rise in the East.

units.mastery_criterion: Students can state that different places have different times because the Sun hits them at different moments.
units.task: Place two labelled locations A and B at different longitudes on a globe model. Rotate the model toward a fixed lamp and compare when each location enters the lit side. Discuss the model limit: clock time is set by conventions as well as longitude.

units.mastery_criterion: Student identifies the dish with growth and explains that invisible organisms from unwashed hands were transferred to it.
units.task: Show the student pictures of two petri dishes from a handwashing experiment (one with spots of bacterial growth, one clean). Ask them to infer which dish was touched by unwashed hands and justify their answer based on the presence of invisible organisms.

units.mastery_criterion: Student's letter includes the reasoning that invisible things can make us sick.
units.task: Students dictate or write a short letter to a friend explaining why they should use soap when washing hands, even if their hands don't look dirty.

units.mastery_criterion: The student selects chemical property and cites the color change or environmental exposure as evidence.
units.task: Show two images on a worksheet: a shiny metal gate and a rusty metal gate. Ask the student to circle if the material changed due to a physical or chemical property, and write one sentence justifying their choice based on the color change.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the apple and the bubbles as chemical changes and justify it using evidence of color change or gas production.
units.task: Students observe a teacher demonstration of baking soda and vinegar creating bubbles. They then look at pictures of cut apples turning brown and melting ice. They discuss in groups and write down which show chemical properties (bubbles, color change) and justify why.

units.mastery_criterion: Student accurately predicts that a higher drop results in more displaced water and justifies it using the concept of mechanical energy.
units.task: Look at a diagram of two identical spheres, one held 20 cm above a cup of water and one held 60 cm above. Predict which sphere will cause more water to spill and explain why using evidence from class experiments.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly predicts the state change and justifies it by referencing the addition or removal of heat.
units.task: Read a short scenario: 'Maria leaves a bowl of ice cubes in the hot sun. What will happen to the ice, and what must she do if she wants to turn that water into a gas?' Write your prediction.

units.mastery_criterion: Students accurately record that higher drops cause higher splashes and write a logical conclusion.
units.task: Students work in pairs with a basin of water and a plastic block. They drop the block from 20 cm, 40 cm, and 60 cm, observing the splash. They use a large piece of chart paper behind the basin to mark how high the water splashed each time. They write a sentence concluding how height affects the splash.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully measure the craters and create a bar graph showing a positive correlation between height and crater size.
units.task: Students model volcanic rocks falling from different heights. Using a sand tray, they drop pumice stones from various measured heights and measure the width of the impact craters. They create a simple bar graph showing crater width versus drop height.

units.mastery_criterion: Students reason that the heat from the lamp caused the liquid water to turn into a gas.
units.task: Compare teacher-supplied time-sequence images and water-level records for two shallow dishes under different warming conditions. Describe the observed change and use the supplied heat-transfer model to explain it. No lamps or heated water are handled.

units.mastery_criterion: Students select the tall tree coconut and justify it by referencing height and energy.
units.task: Read a short scenario: 'A coconut falls from a very tall tree, and another falls from a short tree. Which one will hit the sand with more energy?' Students must write their answer and justify it using evidence from past experiments.

units.mastery_criterion: Student selects the rainy season and justifies it by explaining that intense rain softens the earth, causing the hillside to collapse.
units.task: Read a short description of a landslide blocking a road. Decide during which season (dry or rainy) this is most likely to happen and justify your answer.

units.mastery_criterion: Students select the steep hill and justify it by stating the rain will wash the loose soil down the slope.
units.task: Students are given pictures of different landscapes (a steep hill with no trees, a flat paved area, a riverbank). They must decide which area is most vulnerable to a landslide during the rainy season and justify why.

units.mastery_criterion: Uses the rainfall and river evidence, then states that a season label alone cannot establish that a flood occurred.
units.task: Compare a fictional rainfall record and a diagram of a river near a water pipe. Identify when the supplied record supports concern about flooding, and explain why a season label alone cannot establish that a flood occurred.

units.mastery_criterion: Students deduce that without the extra 6 hours, we would never need to add an extra day to February.
units.task: Students are given a hypothetical scenario: 'What if Earth's orbit took exactly 365 days with no extra hours?' They must write or draw what would happen to our calendar (no leap years).

units.mastery_criterion: Students choose morning, reasoning that Europe is ahead in time and evening there would be too late.
units.task: Students are given a scenario where they must call a relative in Europe. They must decide if they should call during their own morning or evening to ensure the relative is awake, justifying their choice based on rotation.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify fungi by noting they absorb food from decomposing matter.
units.task: Analyze case studies of different organisms and justify if they are plants or fungi based on their food source.

units.mastery_criterion: Student states fungi are not plants and cites their heterotrophic nature and absorptive feeding method.
units.task: Decide whether a mushroom is a plant or not, and justify your answer using evidence about how it gets its food.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify wild animals in the scenarios and justify why they should not be pets.
units.task: Analyze scenarios of finding different animals and justify whether they can be taken home as pets.

units.mastery_criterion: Students articulate that removing animals harms the ecosystem and the animal's well-being.
units.task: Group discussion on the impact of taking wild animals from national protected areas to keep as pets.

units.mastery_criterion: Brochure includes at least one valid reason (e.g., need for space, natural diet) why wild animals shouldn't be pets.
units.task: Create an informational brochure explaining why wild animals are not pets, using evidence about their needs.

units.mastery_criterion: Needs are correctly sorted, demonstrating understanding of the difference in survival strategies.
units.task: Sort a list of animal needs into 'Provided by Humans' (domestic) and 'Found in Nature' (wild).

units.mastery_criterion: Passes if the student decides against keeping the wild animal and provides a justification based on its natural habitat.
units.task: Decide whether a monkey found in the forest should be taken home as a pet. Justify your answer using evidence.

units.mastery_criterion: The student records that the folded bridge holds significantly more coins and justifies that the folds make the paper stiffer.
units.task: Have students place coins one by one on the center of a flat paper bridge until it collapses, then repeat with a fan-folded bridge, and state which design is stronger and why based on data.

units.mastery_criterion: Students record data accurately and reason that more folds generally increase structural resistance up to a point.
units.task: Students experiment with different numbers of folds in their paper bridges (e.g., 2 folds vs. 6 folds) and record how many coins each can hold, justifying which design is best.

units.mastery_criterion: Students justify the folded design's strength using evidence from their block count data.
units.task: Students test flat vs. folded bridges using small blocks instead of coins, simulating a road over a water sanitation channel, and write a justification for the strongest design.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully operate the device and record that more twists result in a longer rolling distance.
units.task: Students experiment with their elastic devices by twisting the rubber band a specific number of times (e.g., 5, 10, 15) and measuring how far the device rolls.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully modify the device, operate it, and observe changes in motion.
units.task: Students modify their elastic devices by adding weight (e.g., taping coins to the tube) to see how mass affects the motion generated by the twisted rubber band.

units.mastery_criterion: The tubes are cut to size and packed tightly enough to stay in place when the can is tilted.
units.task: Ask students to create an insect shelter by cutting paper straws to the length of a recycled can and packing them tightly inside.

units.mastery_criterion: Students adapt their packing technique to the new shape, ensuring materials are secure and provide hollow spaces.
units.task: Students build a second insect hotel using a different container shape (e.g., a square milk carton) and natural materials like hollow twigs, ensuring tight packing.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully attach natural camouflage to the exterior without blocking the hollow tube entrances.
units.task: Students decorate the outside of their insect hotels using natural materials (leaves, bark) glued to the exterior to help it blend into a natural environment.

units.mastery_criterion: The chosen location is low-traffic and the justification explicitly mentions avoiding disturbance to the insects.
units.task: Ask students to choose a location in the schoolyard or at home to place their insect hotel and write one sentence explaining why that location is best for the insects.

units.mastery_criterion: Students select a viable low-traffic spot and note its quiet nature on their map.
units.task: Take students on a walk around the schoolyard. Have them select a specific spot for their insect hotel and draw a map marking the location, noting why it is low-traffic.

units.mastery_criterion: Students place the 'X' away from paths and playgrounds, justifying it with the need to avoid disturbance.
units.task: Students review a map of a hypothetical park and mark an 'X' where they would place an insect hotel, writing a justification based on avoiding human paths.

units.mastery_criterion: The terrarium has distinct layers (rocks then soil) and the plant is securely placed in the soil with roots covered.
units.task: Provide students with a clear plastic container, small rocks, soil, and a small plant. Ask them to assemble a terrarium that supports the plant's growth.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully water the plant without flooding it, observing the drainage layer's function.
units.task: Students add decorative elements (small plastic animals, colored stones) to their terrariums and lightly water the soil, observing how the water drains into the rock layer.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly layer rocks and soil, and plant the seed at the correct depth.
units.task: Students build a second, smaller terrarium using a plastic cup, focusing on planting a seed (like maize) instead of a live plant, ensuring the soil depth is appropriate.

units.mastery_criterion: Student draws or writes about a recognized safety measure for floods, such as moving to higher ground.
units.task: Present a novel scenario: a heavy rainstorm causes a flood warning near their home. Students draw or write one safe action they should take in this specific context.

units.mastery_criterion: Student selects the bare dirt hill and provides a logical justification involving the lack of roots to hold the soil.
units.task: Show the student a picture of a steep, bare dirt hill and a picture of a hill covered in grass and trees. Ask them to predict which hill will lose more soil during a heavy rainstorm and explain why using their knowledge of roots.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly connects the apple core and banana peel to biodegradable, and the plastic bottle and glass jar to non-biodegradable.
units.task: Provide a worksheet with images of an apple core, plastic bottle, glass jar, and banana peel. Students draw a line connecting each item to the correct bin (Biodegradable or Non-biodegradable).

units.mastery_criterion: Student reacts promptly and correctly assumes the safe position without prompting.
units.task: Role-play activity: The teacher calls out 'Earthquake!' at random times during a 30-minute period. Students must immediately execute the safe action.

units.mastery_criterion: Student's comic accurately depicts a recognized safety measure in the middle panel.
units.task: Students create a simple three-panel comic strip showing a character feeling an earthquake, taking cover, and waiting safely.

units.mastery_criterion: Student places the evacuation steps in a logical, safe order for the given hazard.
units.task: Students sequence a set of mixed-up picture cards showing the steps of an emergency evacuation plan for various hazards, including earthquakes, floods, and landslides.

units.mastery_criterion: Student infers that a steeper angle causes more soil to wash away, but plants still offer the best protection.
units.task: Students repeat the erosion model experiment, but this time they tilt the bottles at a steeper angle to simulate a steep hill. They observe and discuss how the angle affects the amount of soil washed away.

units.mastery_criterion: Student reasons that faster water flow carries more soil away.
units.task: Students test the erosion model by pouring water very slowly (light rain) versus very quickly (heavy storm) into the bare soil bottle, comparing the runoff.

units.mastery_criterion: Student observes and states which soil type resulted in dirtier runoff water.
units.task: Students compare the erosion of regular garden soil versus sandy soil in the bare-soil model, observing which washes away faster.

units.mastery_criterion: Student infers that soap is needed to properly remove the 'invisible organisms' represented by the cinnamon.
units.task: Students work in pairs. One applies the oil and cinnamon 'germs'. They test washing with cold water only, warm water only, and finally soap and water, observing which method removes the 'germs' best and inferring why soap is essential.

units.mastery_criterion: Student's sentence justifies handwashing by mentioning the removal of organisms or germs.
units.task: Students trace their hand on paper and draw tiny 'invisible organisms' all over it, then write one sentence at the bottom explaining why they need to wash them off.

units.mastery_criterion: Student places their assigned cards in the correct hoops.
units.task: Relay race: Students pick a picture card of a waste item from a pile and run to drop it in the correct biodegradable or non-biodegradable hoop.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes at least 5 items on their T-chart.
units.task: Students cut out pictures of various items from old magazines and paste them onto a T-chart labeled Biodegradable and Non-Biodegradable.

units.mastery_criterion: Student includes only biodegradable items (like fruit peels, leaves, paper) on their mobile.
units.task: Students create a hanging mobile using only drawings of biodegradable items, reinforcing what belongs in that specific category.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly measure and sequence the strings based on their centimeter length.
units.task: Provide students with pieces of string of different lengths. They must measure the string in centimeters and order them from shortest to longest on their desks.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully test materials and correctly categorize them as conductors or insulators based on the LED lighting up.
units.task: Students test various materials (rubber bands, cloth, foil, paper, paperclips) by placing them in a gap in a simple 1.5V battery circuit to see if the LED lights up. They categorize the materials as conductors or insulators based on whether they block or allow electricity to flow.

units.mastery_criterion: Students identify at least 3 objects and correctly state their energy transformations.
units.task: Classroom scavenger hunt. Students walk around the room with a clipboard to find 5 objects that transform energy (e.g., pencil sharpener, clock, light switch). They draw the object and write what energy it uses and what it turns into.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully mix the primary colors to create green, red, and brown for their painting.
units.task: Paint a pattern containing green circles, red triangles and brown rectangles using only cyan, magenta and yellow paint. Record each mixture and adjust one unsuccessful mixture using the observed result.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully build a sequence and correctly label at least two energy transformations.
units.task: Students build a simple sequence using safe classroom objects (e.g., a toy car rolling down a ramp to hit a bell). They draw their sequence and label the energy transformations happening at each step (e.g., potential to kinetic, kinetic to sound).

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort all 5 items based on memory of material properties.
units.task: Flashback activity: Provide a quick sorting tray with 5 small items (coin, clear plastic cup, wooden block, tissue paper, glass marble). Students must quickly sort them into 'Shadow Makers' and 'Light Passers' based on previous lessons.

units.mastery_criterion: Students select clear plastic and justify it by stating it lets light pass through.
units.task: Read a scenario: 'We need to build a greenhouse to help plants grow. Should we use wood or clear plastic for the roof? Why?' Students write their answer recalling that plants need light to pass through.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully group the four 6-hour cubes to demonstrate the creation of the extra day.
units.task: Students work in groups with linking cubes. They build four towers of 365 cubes (represented by a large block) and add one small cube (6 hours) to each. They then combine the 4 small cubes to make a 'new day' block.

units.mastery_criterion: Students link planting activities that need water to the rainy season.
units.task: Given a fictional plant requirement card and monthly rainfall data, choose a period that meets the supplied water requirement and justify it. Do not prescribe real crop planting dates from a simplified chart.

units.mastery_criterion: Drawings accurately reflect the environmental conditions and appropriate clothing for both local seasons.
units.task: Students create a two-panel drawing. On one side, they draw their school during the dry season; on the other, during the rainy season, including appropriate clothing for themselves in the drawing.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully demonstrate both rotation and revolution simultaneously without confusing the two.
units.task: Students create a floor model of the orbit. One student stands in the center as the Sun. Another student holds a globe and walks the orbital path, ensuring they also spin the globe (rotation) while walking (revolution).

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly inserts the axis and spins the model in place, stating the skewer is the imaginary axis.
units.task: Use a teacher-preassembled globe or foam-ball model with a blunt paper-tube axis. Demonstrate rotation and point to the imaginary axis. Students do not pierce or assemble the model.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully assemble the model and spin it in place rather than moving it in a circle.
units.task: Use preassembled models made by the teacher with a foam ball and a blunt paper tube. In pairs, demonstrate spinning in place and point to the rotation axis. Students do not pierce or assemble the models.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify opposite ends of the spheres as the poles where the imaginary axis would pass through.
units.task: Students are given various spherical objects (a plastic ball, a crumpled paper ball, a clay sphere) and must identify where the imaginary axis would be by drawing a line or placing a sticker on the 'poles'.

units.mastery_criterion: Students draw a vertical or slightly tilted line through the center of both the top and the Earth model in their diagrams.
units.task: Students compare a spinning top to their Earth model. They spin the top on their desks and draw a diagram showing the imaginary axis of the top compared to the Earth model.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the lit area as day and the shadowed area as night while rotating the globe, keeping the flashlight still.
units.task: Using a flashlight to represent the Sun and a globe for Earth, show why it is daytime in one country and nighttime in another by rotating the globe.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly rotate the ball in place while keeping the light source stationary, identifying day and night areas.
units.task: In pairs, students use a small ball on a stick and a small flashlight. One student holds the 'Sun' steady while the other rotates the 'Earth', observing how the light hits the surface.

units.mastery_criterion: The half of the Earth facing the light source is colored brightly, and the opposite half is colored darkly.
units.task: Students are given a worksheet with a drawing of the Sun and the Earth. They must color the side of the Earth facing the Sun yellow (day) and the side facing away black or dark blue (night).

units.mastery_criterion: Students draw long shadows on opposite sides of the block for morning and evening.
units.task: Students use a small block (representing a building) on a piece of paper. Using a flashlight moving in an arc (to simulate the apparent motion caused by rotation), they trace the shadow of the block in the 'morning' and 'evening'.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify that their left side (representing East) enters the light before their face.
units.task: Students stand in a circle around a central lamp (Sun). They slowly rotate their bodies to the left (West to East) and note which shoulder (East) sees the light first.

units.mastery_criterion: Student states it is later in Spain because it is to the East and rotated into the sunlight before El Salvador.
units.task: Use a supplied simplified time-zone map with locations A and B and an explicit offset. Determine which location has the later clock reading using that offset.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify that the country to the East experiences morning (and breakfast) first.
units.task: Use two labelled locations at different longitudes on a supplied globe diagram. Apply the given rotation direction and compare which enters the lit side first.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly deduce that zones to the East are later in the day.
units.task: Students look at a simplified, color-coded time zone map. They answer questions like: 'If it is noon in the red zone, is it morning or afternoon in the blue zone to the East?'

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly categorize their selected local plants into the three utility groups.
units.task: Create a shopping list for a local market, selecting plants and categorizing them into food, medicine, and raw materials.

units.mastery_criterion: Poster accurately places at least two local crops into their correct utility categories.
units.task: Create a poster classifying local crops into food, medicine, and raw materials.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully match all plant cards to their correct utility category.
units.task: Play a matching game where students pair a plant with the human need it satisfies (e.g., aloe for medicine, wood for building).

units.mastery_criterion: Items are correctly sorted into food, medicine, or raw materials based on their plant origin.
units.task: Sort a mixed basket of everyday items (e.g., wooden spoon, herbal tea box, apple) into plant utility categories.

units.mastery_criterion: Passes if all provided plants are placed in a plausible utility category.
units.task: Sort a provided list of plants (e.g., corn, mint, cotton) into categories: food, medicine, and raw materials.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly match the local animal to its movement and body part.
units.task: Match supplied animal pictures to their primary movement method and identify the body part used.

units.mastery_criterion: The drawn animal has clear body parts (e.g., wings) that match the student's stated locomotion method.
units.task: Design an imaginary animal with specific body parts adapted for a chosen method of locomotion.

units.mastery_criterion: Cards are sorted correctly and the correct body part is circled on each.
units.task: Sort animal picture cards by locomotion type and circle the body part that allows it using a dry-erase marker.

units.mastery_criterion: Chart accurately categorizes animals and lists fins, wings, and legs respectively.
units.task: Create a chart categorizing animals into swimmers, flyers, and walkers, listing the key body part for each group.

units.mastery_criterion: Passes if unfamiliar animals are matched correctly with the corresponding body part identified.
units.task: Given pictures of unfamiliar animals (e.g., an axolotl, an ostrich), infer their primary movement method and circle the body part.

units.mastery_criterion: Animals are correctly placed into herbivore, carnivore, or omnivore categories.
units.task: Classify a list of animals into diet categories based on short written descriptions of what they eat.

units.mastery_criterion: Menus accurately reflect plant-based foods for herbivores, meat for carnivores, and both for omnivores.
units.task: Create a restaurant menu for different animal types, ensuring the food items match their specific diet classification.

units.mastery_criterion: All cards/cutouts are placed in the correct diet zone based on prior knowledge of their diets.
units.task: Sort printed animal cards or student-drawn cutouts into three distinct habitat zones labeled Herbivore, Carnivore, and Omnivore.

units.mastery_criterion: Cards are sorted correctly within the time limit.
units.task: Quick sorting of animal diet cards into three piles: herbivore, carnivore, omnivore.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly fill in herbivore, carnivore, or omnivore for each item.
units.task: Fill-in-the-blank worksheet where students write the correct diet classification next to an animal's name and food source.

units.mastery_criterion: Passes if all three animals are correctly classified according to their described diets.
units.task: Read the descriptions of what a cow, a lion, and a bear eat. Classify each as a herbivore, carnivore, or omnivore.

units.mastery_criterion: Rules directly address mitigating human threats (e.g., no littering, stay on trails).
units.task: Draft a set of rules for visitors to national protected areas to ensure wild animals are protected.

units.mastery_criterion: Students acting as rangers clearly state a rule that protects wildlife during the role-play.
units.task: Role-play park rangers explaining conservation rules to visitors who are acting carelessly.

units.mastery_criterion: Sign includes a clear visual and text rule that protects wildlife.
units.task: Design a warning sign for a forest to remind people how to protect the animals living there.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly match the consequence and propose a protective alternative action.
units.task: Match scenarios of human actions in nature to their consequences for wildlife, then propose a better action.

units.mastery_criterion: Passes if the response correctly identifies the harm of feeding wild animals and proposes a safe alternative like observing.
units.task: Read a scenario where a visitor wants to feed a wild animal. Write a response explaining why they shouldn't and what they should do instead.

units.mastery_criterion: The recorded measurement is within 1 cm of the actual circumference and the string method is used correctly.
units.task: Provide students with a spherical fruit, a piece of string, and a ruler. Ask them to determine the distance around the thickest part of the fruit and record the measurement in centimeters.

units.mastery_criterion: Students record at least 5 accurate measurements, demonstrating proper string alignment and ruler usage.
units.task: Students work in pairs to measure the circumference of various classroom objects (globes, balls, thick markers) using string and rulers, recording their data in a table.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the crop with the largest circumference based on their accurate string measurements.
units.task: Students measure the circumference of different local crops (like small pumpkins or large maize cobs) using string and rulers to determine which crop has the largest girth.

units.mastery_criterion: The balance is constructed symmetrically and the student correctly identifies the equilibrium point with the correct number of marbles.
units.task: Ask students to build a balance using a clothes hanger, string, and two cups, and then determine how many marbles equal the mass of a small eraser.

units.mastery_criterion: Students accurately record the number of marbles required to balance at least 4 different objects.
units.task: Students use their constructed balances to compare the mass of various classroom items (erasers, pencils, glue sticks) against a standard non-standard unit (marbles), recording the equivalents.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully balance the items with coins and record the mass in 'coin units'.
units.task: Use a balance to compare the masses of two supplied objects using identical counters as a non-standard unit. Record the counter counts; do not infer mass from monetary value.

units.mastery_criterion: Students assemble the balance correctly and achieve equilibrium within the time limit.
units.task: Students quickly reassemble a balance from disassembled parts and verify its equilibrium using identical wooden blocks.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly add beads one by one until the hanger is level.
units.task: Students use a pre-made balance to find the mass of a small rock in terms of plastic beads, recalling the procedure for achieving equilibrium.

units.mastery_criterion: The device is assembled correctly and demonstrates motion upon release.
units.task: Instruct students to build a rolling device using CDs, a cardboard tube, and rubber bands, twist the rubber band mechanism, and release it on the floor to demonstrate motion.

units.mastery_criterion: All four items are placed in the correct categories.
units.task: Provide a worksheet with a list of words and pictures: dog, rock, tree, bicycle. Ask the student to draw a line to sort them into Living and Non-living boxes.

units.mastery_criterion: Drawings show progression: a plain seed, a seed with a small root, and a seed with a larger sprout/leaves.
units.task: Provide a worksheet with three blank boxes labeled Day 1, Day 3, and Day 5. Ask the student to draw the changes in a germinating bean seed based on what they learned.

units.mastery_criterion: One point for the correct stimulus-response match and one for identifying the before/after evidence; both are required.
units.task: Use only teacher-supplied picture pairs and fictional before/after records. Match a supplied change in lighting or movement with the response shown in two fictional records. Cite one visible change.

units.mastery_criterion: All four properties are sorted into the correct categories.
units.task: Provide a worksheet with a list of properties: red, 15 cm, heavy, 30 degrees. Ask the student to write them into Qualitative and Quantitative columns.

units.mastery_criterion: The student correctly identifies the object in the cup that goes down as having more mass.
units.task: Conduct a whole-class demonstration using a balance scale. Place an eraser and a sharpener in the cups. Ask students to independently record on their worksheet which object has more mass based on which cup goes down.

units.mastery_criterion: The student writes the correct measurement within 0.5 cm of the actual length and includes cm for all five lines.
units.task: Give students a worksheet with five printed lines of varying lengths and a ruler. Ask them to measure each line and write the length in centimeters next to it.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly classify at least 10 out of 12 hidden items into the correct categories.
units.task: Simulate a nature walk using large posters of national protected areas around the room. Students walk around with a clipboard, finding hidden picture cards of entities (animals, plants, rocks, water) and sorting them into a living/non-living T-chart.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sequence the 4 stages of germination.
units.task: Students are given a set of mixed-up picture cards showing the stages of maize germination. They must sequence them in the correct order from dry seed to small plant, and glue them into their notebooks.

units.mastery_criterion: One point for the correct stimulus-response match and one for identifying the before/after evidence; both are required.
units.task: Use only teacher-supplied picture pairs and fictional before/after records. Match a supplied change in lighting or movement with the response shown in two fictional records. Cite one visible change.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly sort at least 15 out of 20 property cards and can justify one of each type.
units.task: Students receive a deck of cards with various properties written and illustrated on them. In pairs, they must sort the cards into Qualitative and Quantitative piles, justifying their choices to each other.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify and record the heavier object for at least 5 pairs using the balance scale.
units.task: Students work in small groups with a balance scale. They are given pairs of classroom items (e.g., marker vs crayon, scissors vs glue stick). They predict which has more mass, test it, and record the results.

units.mastery_criterion: Students accurately measure and record the lengths of at least 8 images within 0.5 cm accuracy.
units.task: Students work in pairs to measure the length of various printed images of local crops (maize leaves, sugarcane sticks) using a ruler. They record the measurements in centimeters in a structured table.

units.mastery_criterion: Students record at least three accurate qualitative properties for each of the five objects.
units.task: Set up five observation stations with different everyday materials. Students rotate through the stations, observing the objects and recording three qualitative properties (color, texture, smell) for each in their notebooks.

units.mastery_criterion: Students independently select and correctly categorize four images.
units.task: Give students old magazines. They must cut out two pictures of living things and two pictures of non-living things, and glue them onto a divided paper.

units.mastery_criterion: Students independently align the ruler and read the correct centimeter value.
units.task: Students retrieve their rulers and measure the length of their own pencils and erasers, recording the values on a sticky note to place on a class chart.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the category for 8 out of 10 called items.
units.task: Conduct a whiteboard relay. Call out an item (e.g., cloud, bird, volcano, grass). Students write L for living or N for non-living on their personal whiteboards and hold them up.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes 4 out of 5 given materials into conductors and insulators.
units.task: Sort a list of materials (copper wire, plastic spoon, human body, rubber eraser, iron nail) into two columns: 'Conducts Electricity' and 'Blocks Electricity'.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches at least 3 out of 4 scenarios to their energy transformation.
units.task: Draw lines to connect the object (e.g., a fan plugged into a wall, a child sliding down a slide) to the correct energy change (e.g., electrical to mechanical, potential to kinetic).

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes 4 out of 5 materials as light-blocking (opaque) or light-passing (transparent/translucent).
units.task: Given a list of items (a thick book, a clear glass window, a wooden door, a piece of clear cellophane, a metal spoon), sort them into a table with two columns: 'Forms a dark shadow' and 'Lets light pass through'.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly test and classify at least 8 out of 10 objects.
units.task: Station rotation: Students use safe 1.5V battery circuits to test 10 different classroom objects (eraser, foil, copper wire, wooden block, etc.). They record their predictions and actual results in a T-chart labeled 'Conductors' and 'Insulators'.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully match all pairs and articulate the transformation happening.
units.task: Students play a matching card game in pairs. They must match a 'Before' card (e.g., a battery, a wound-up spring) with an 'After' card (e.g., a moving toy car, a spinning fan) and state the energy transformation out loud to their partner.

units.mastery_criterion: Students successfully combine opaque and translucent materials to create a functional shadow puppet.
units.task: Students create a shadow puppet theater. They are given black cardboard (opaque) and colored tissue paper (translucent). They must design a puppet that has both a solid shadow body and glowing colored eyes/features. They test their puppets behind a sheet with a flashlight.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly apply green for safe routes and red for hazards on their map.
units.task: Apply a supplied red/green sign code to a fictional floor-plan drawing with marked obstacles and a marked clear route. Compare the coding with a partner and justify one choice using the key.

units.mastery_criterion: Identifies the lower- and higher-rainfall periods and cites relative values from the supplied chart.
units.task: Use a supplied rainfall chart to name a sustained drier period and a sustained wetter period. Cite one difference in the data.

units.mastery_criterion: The student states that electrical energy from the battery is changing into thermal energy (heat) in the pencil lead, using the melting wax as evidence.
units.task: Show students a safe, teacher-led demonstration of a battery connected to a pencil lead with a small piece of wax on it. Ask them to observe the wax melting and name the type of energy transformation occurring.

units.mastery_criterion: Students correctly identify the food source (human provided vs. independently found).
units.task: Compare supplied pictures and habitat records for one domestic and one wild animal. Draw each and describe how it obtains food using the supplied evidence.

units.mastery_criterion: Student circles a spilled liquid, an open cabinet door, and a tripping hazard.
units.task: Provide a worksheet with an image of a messy kitchen. Students must independently circle three things that could cause an accident.

units.mastery_criterion: Student circles the raw chicken and raw beans.
units.task: Provide a worksheet with images of raw chicken, an apple, and raw beans. Students circle the ones that must be cooked before eating.

units.mastery_criterion: Student selects the option defining risk as the probability of suffering harmful consequences.
units.task: Students complete a multiple-choice question selecting the correct definition of 'risk' from three options.

units.mastery_criterion: Student marks a sad face for 'Not washing hands after going to the bathroom'.
units.task: Read a list of actions aloud. Students mark a sad face on their paper next to the number if the action represents poor hygiene.

units.mastery_criterion: Student writes that a vaccine helps the body make defenses or fight off sickness.
units.task: Ask the student to write one sentence explaining what a vaccine does inside the body.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly sorts all unsafe situation cards into the risk pile.
units.task: Students sort illustrated cards into two piles: safe situations and unsafe situations (risks).

units.mastery_criterion: Student circles at least three distinct risks across the provided photographs.
units.task: Students view photographs of different rooms in a house and circle the accident risks using a dry-erase marker.

units.mastery_criterion: Student successfully draws three recognizable risks and identifies the risks in their partner's drawing.
units.task: Students draw a picture of a playground and intentionally include three accident risks, then trade with a partner to find them.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly places items like play-chicken in the 'Must be cooked' basket.
units.task: Students sort plastic play-food into two baskets: 'Safe to eat raw (after washing)' and 'Must be cooked'.

units.mastery_criterion: Student draws and correctly identifies which of their drawn items needs cooking.
units.task: Students draw a 'safe menu' consisting of one item that can be eaten raw and one item that must be cooked, labeling them appropriately.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly matches the raw ingredients to their cooked counterparts.
units.task: Matching game: Students match a picture of a raw ingredient (like raw meat or raw dough) to its safe, cooked final dish.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly categorizes at least four food items.
units.task: Students create a 'safe kitchen' poster by cutting out pictures of food and gluing them under 'Wash and Eat' or 'Cook First' headings.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly pairs the hazard cards with their corresponding risk definition cards.
units.task: Students match cards showing a natural event (hazard) with cards showing the probability of harm (risk) based on human location.

units.mastery_criterion: Student holds up the correct card for at least 4 out of 5 scenarios.
units.task: Read fictional cards describing a hazardous event and cards describing exposure to that event. Sort event and exposure cards, then justify one pairing.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly circles the poor hygiene practices (e.g., sneezing into hands, not washing hands).
units.task: Show a series of pictures depicting daily routines. Students must spot and circle the 'mistake' (the poor hygiene practice) in each picture.

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the acted-out habit as poor hygiene when applicable.
units.task: Play a game of charades where students act out either a good hygiene habit or a poor hygiene habit. The class guesses the action and states if it is good or poor.

units.mastery_criterion: Student places cards like 'not washing hands' into the 'Can make us sick' pile.
units.task: Students sort a deck of cards showing various actions into a 'Keeps us healthy' pile and a 'Can make us sick' pile.

units.mastery_criterion: Student's drawing reflects the concept of protection or defense inside the body.
units.task: Students draw a picture of their body's 'defenses' (like tiny shields or guards) stopping sickness, based on the vaccine metaphor.

units.mastery_criterion: Student places the pictures in the correct chronological order.
units.task: Students sequence three pictures: 1) Getting a vaccine, 2) Body making defenses, 3) Staying healthy when sickness is around.

units.mastery_criterion: Student can explain their role as a defense created by the vaccine.
units.task: Students role-play as 'body guards' (defenses) learning to recognize a 'villain' (sickness) after being trained by a 'teacher' (vaccine).

units.mastery_criterion: Student correctly identifies the difference through physical movement.
units.task: Quick recall game: The teacher says a word (either a hazard like 'rain' or a risk like 'flooded house'). Students stand up for hazard, sit down for risk.

units.mastery_criterion: Student's sentence includes the concept of probability of harm or getting hurt.
units.task: Exit ticket: Students write or dictate one sentence explaining what a risk is before leaving for recess.

units.mastery_criterion: Student recalls a relevant word associated with vaccine function.
units.task: Pass a soft ball around a circle. When the music stops, the student holding the ball must say one word related to what vaccines do (e.g., 'defenses', 'protect', 'fight').

units.mastery_criterion: Student fills in the blank with 'defenses' or a similar accurate term.
units.task: Provide a quick fill-in-the-blank slip: 'A vaccine helps the body make ________ to fight sickness.'
